headline: Mei, “niece”, is attested in the Ryūnoshūge of 738, and its initial me- is often associated with 女 (me, “female”).

sources.quote: From Old Japanese; attested in the Ryūnoshūge (738) as 売比 ⟨me₁ pi₁⟩.
* ⟨me₁ pi₁⟩ → /mefi/ → /mei/
The initial me- has been frequently associated with 女 (me, “female”).

headline: Masu, “to increase”, is simply from Old Japanese ます.

sources.quote: From Old Japanese ます (“to increase”).

headline: Onegai shimasu is 御 (o-) plus 願う (negau, “request, implore”) plus します, the formal form of する (suru).

sources.quote: From 御(お) (o-) + 願(ねが)う (negau, “request, implore”) + します (shimasu, a polite honorific (丁(てい)寧(ねい)語(ご) (teineigo)) formula used to show respect to the hearer). The latter portion is the formal or socially distanced form of する (suru). See also ます (-masu, suffix).

headline: Wareware is a reduplication of 我 (ware, “I; me”).

sources.quote: Reduplication of 我 (ware, “I; me”).

headline: Zenkoku is Middle Chinese 全國, literally “whole country”, first attested in the mid-1800s.

sources.quote: From Middle Chinese 全國 (MC dzjwen kwok, literally “whole country”).
First attested in the mid-1800s.

headline: Ni tsuite is に (ni, “to”) plus ついて (tsuite), the -te form of the verb 就く (tsuku).

sources.quote: に (ni, “to”, a particle which modifies the previous word) + ついて (tsuite, -te conjunctive form of the verb 就く (tsuku))

headline: Tsumori is the continuative stem of 積もる (tsumoru, “to intend”).

sources.quote: 連(れん)用(よう)形(けい) (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of the verb 積(つ)もる (tsumoru, “to intend”).

headline: Naosu is derived from 直 (nao, “straight; common, normal, ordinary”) plus a transitive suffix, and is cognate with 治す (naosu, “to cure, to heal”).

sources.quote: Transitive verb derived from 直(なお) (nao, “straight; common, normal, ordinary”) + transitive / causative suffixing element す (su). Cognate with 治(なお)す (naosu, “to cure, to heal”).

headline: Shinshin is 心 (shin, “heart”) plus 身 (shin, “body”): the same reading twice.

sources.quote: From 心 (shin, “heart”) + 身 (shin, “body”).

headline: Gōka is Middle Chinese 豪華, literally “grand + flowery”.

sources.quote: From Middle Chinese 豪華 (MC haw hwae|xwae|hwaeH, literally “grand + flowery”). Compare modern Cantonese reading hou⁴ waa⁴.

headline: Sumi is first attested in the Nihon Shoki of 720 CE with the phonetic spelling 須彌, and is cognate with 炭 (sumi, “charcoal”).

sources.quote: From Old Japanese, first appearing in the Nihon Shoki of 720 CE with the phonetic spelling 須彌 ⟨sumi₁⟩. Cognate with 炭 (sumi, “charcoal”).
In turn, from Proto-Japonic *sumi. Cognate with Southern Amami Ōshima 墨 (sïmi).

Possibly derived from the homophonous 連用形 (ren'yōkei, “continuative or stem form”) 済み (sumi) of verb 済む (sumu, “to finish, to conclude”), from the way that cinders are left after a fire has finished burning.
Possibly also related to 煤 (susu, “soot”), from which India ink is made.

headline: Kagiri is the continuative stem of 限る (kagiru, “to limit, to restrict”).

sources.quote: From the 連(れん)用(よう)形(けい) (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of the verb 限(かぎ)る (kagiru, “to limit, to restrict”).

meaning: humble form of 行く (いく), 聞く (きく) and 来る (くる)
headline: Ukagau is a doublet of 窺う (ukagau, “to peek”).

sources.quote: Doublet of 窺(うかが)う (ukagau, “to peek”).

headline: Mō has an unknown derivation; it was originally まう (mau), first attested in 1477.

sources.quote: Derivation unknown. First attested in 1477, around the Muromachi Period.

Historical kana orthography shows that this was originally まう (mau), and Portuguese sources from the late 1500s and early 1600s record this as ⟨mǒ⟩, indicating a pronunciation of /mɔː/ as part of the regular sound shift from /au/ to /oː/.

The initial ma is speculatively connected to 今 (ima, “now”) (compare both the loss of initial i- in 未だ (imada > mada) or 出る (ideru > deru) and the similar -a → -ō shift seen in emphatic particle のう (nō)). Frellesvig suggests a shift from a topicalized form /ima wa/ → /mau/ → /mɔː/ → /moː/.

headline: Kindai is 近 (“near”) plus 代 (“age; period”).

sources.quote: 近 (“near”) + 代 (“age; period”)

headline: Ou is perhaps cognate with 負う (ou, “to carry on the back”), as both involve one person moving behind another, though the accents do not match.

sources.quote: From Old Japanese, from Proto-Japonic *op- ~ əp-. Perhaps cognate with 負う (ou, “to carry on the back”), as both words involve the movement of one person behind another person, but the accent values in Early Middle Japanese and Kyoto do not match.

headline: Ken, “ticket”, went from kwen to ken, from Middle Chinese 券 (MC khjwonH, “ticket”).

sources.quote: /kwen/ → /ken/
From Middle Chinese 券 (MC khjwonH, “ticket”).

sources.quote: Compound of 乗り (nori, “getting on, riding”, from verb 乗る noru “to ride, to be on top of”) + 換える (kaeru, “to exchange, to change”).

headline: Sate is compared with さして (sashite, “(not) to such an extent”), and its page notes the readings さす (sasu) of kanji 扨 and 扠.

sources.quote: Compare さして (sashite, “(not) to such an extent”), from 然(さ) (sa), and さして (sashite, conjunctive form of さす (sasu)). For the latter, note readings さす (sasu) of kanji 扨 and 扠, also alternative spellings of this term.

sources.quote: Cognate with Japanese 開(あ)ける (akeru, “to open”) and 空(あ)ける (akeru, “to empty”).

headline: Yomi is the continuative stem of 読む (yomu, “to read”).

sources.quote: The 連(れん)用(よう)形(けい) (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of the verb 読(よ)む (yomu, “to read”).

headline: Sode, “sleeve”, appears to be 衣 (so, “robe; clothing”) plus 手 (te, “hand; arm”), first attested in the Kojiki of 712.

sources.quote: ⟨so₁ te⟩ → /so te/ → /sode/
From Old Japanese. First attested in the Kojiki of 712 with the phonetic spelling 蘇弖 (⟨so₁ te⟩). The te changes to de as an instance of rendaku (連濁).

Japanese references that include an etymology note that this appears to be a compound of 衣 (so, “robe; clothing”) + 手 (te, “hand; arm”). However, the initial so- is clearly spelled with the so-called 甲類 (kōrui, “"A" type”) vowel ⟨so₁⟩ in the oldest texts, whereas 衣 when read as so was pronounced with the so-called 乙類 (otsurui, “"B" type”) vowel as ⟨so₂⟩. These were treated as separate vowels in Old Japanese, so this proposed compound cannot be the actual derivation.

headline: Fushigi is contracted from 不可思議 (fuka shigi, literally “unfathomable”).

sources.quote: Contracted from 不(ふ)可(か)思(し)議(ぎ) (fuka shigi, literally “unfathomable”); equivalent to 不(ふ) (fu-) + 思議(しぎ) (shigi).
